newsitem.title: UK: Confidence builds in Euro shares post "grey Friday".
newsitem.headline: Confidence builds in Euro shares post "grey Friday".

text.p: Steep losses suffered by European bourses on "grey Friday" struck fear into investors' hearts last week, but pundits say confidence is returning and forecast further share gains despite lingering worries over Wall Street.
"The underlying outlook for both U.S. and European stock markets is still robust," said Peter Chambers, chief investment strategist at HSBC James Capel.
Global stock markets plunged last Friday after US Federal Reserve chief Alan Greenspan warned of "irrational exuberance" escalating asset values.
The warning wiped billion of dollars off all major bourses amid speculation that Greenspan was paving the way for a rise in U.S. interest rates.
A rebound in European share prices across Europe on Monday met some resistance on Tuesday and shares ended lower in Paris and Amsterdam as a cautious mood prevailed.

But in Frankfurt and London shares advanced, the DAX index rose 1.18 percent or 33.76 points to 2,891 amid dealers' hopes that a rebound to 2,900 would trigger fresh buying interest and the FTSE 100 closed up 24.1 points at 4,035.7, within striking distance of its all-time highs.
Market experts are agreed that a period of volatility is likely as investors were unnerved by the speed and ferocity of Friday's plunge but that need not prevent longer term gains.
"Calm is restored, the memories will fade in the next couple of weeks," said David Rough, managing director investments, Legal & General, which manages 40 billion pounds of assets.

"For people who wanted to panic, Greenspan gave them a good excuse to sell and the speed of the decline confirms markets will remain volatile," Rough said but added that he saw the UK market as less vulnerable than most.
A spokesman for M&G in London which controls 15 billion pounds of assets said their view was that the US market remained expensive but it would not change its investment stance.
"We've seen a number of corrections and there's still resilience in the markets," he added.
Strategists and investors see several supporting factors, principally that comparing European shares to U.S. shares, market valuations are less stretched and corporate earnings expectations brighter.

On Wall Street the Dow has advanced by some 28 percent since the start of the year. Compared to this the FTSE 100 has risen just nine percent so far this year with a further nine percent gain forecast for 1997, according to a Reuter poll.
However, substantial gains have also been achieved in Amsterdam where the AEX Index of 25 leading Dutch shares is up some 28 percent and generally regarded as fairly valued.
However ING Barings general strategist Philip Menco said:"It's moving around it's long-term trend. We think it could go higher."
He added that if Greenspan repeated his comments of last Friday, they would be shrugged off.
The German DAX index of leading shares has risen some 27 percent since the end of 1995 and local views are divided over whether valuations are stretched at current levels.
But most analysts say the DAX has room to climb further next year to 3,000 point-level and beyond and stress that Friday's fall helped take some of steam out of market.
"We had risen too fast and overheated...some profit-taking and consolidation can only be healthy for the market," said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist, Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt.
Chambers pointed to Germany as having the strongest corporate earnings outlook on the Continent for 1997, but said this would be outpaced by 12 percent growth in the U.K.
"For the United States we have only factored in five percent earnings growth across the market," Chambers added.
But Lehman Brothers strategist Joe Rooney disputed that US earnings growth would be significantly lower than European and stuck to his overweight stance on the United States.
He also cautioned that the high dividend payout ratio of markets like the UK, which has won it investors favour, was a longer-term concern as it raised questions over companies' investment.
